claims.text: The initially solid FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles have a nominally uniform elemental distribution.
Approaching the premelting regime enhances atomic or surface diffusion in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
Enhanced diffusion causes Cu to segregate preferentially to the nanoparticle exterior.
Cu migrates preferentially to the surface because it has a lower melting point.
Cu accumulation produces a Cu-enriched surface layer with a lower melting temperature than the remaining core.
The Cu-enriched surface layer becomes liquid-like below the full melting temperature of the nanoparticle.
Localized surface premelting promotes progressive inward melting in a core-shell sequence.
A pre-annealing homogenization treatment suppresses Cu surface segregation.
Suppressing Cu segregation delays localized premelting and raises the apparent melting temperature.
Untreated nanoparticles will develop localized Cu-rich, liquid-like surface regions in the premelting regime.
Pre-annealed nanoparticles will remain compositionally homogeneous and solid to higher temperatures than untreated nanoparticles.
In situ electron-microscope heating can monitor nanoparticle stability and reveal whether elemental segregation accompanies heating.
TEM-EDS and ex situ APT can establish the surface-to-core Cu distribution and help distinguish thermal segregation from electron-beam artifacts.
An argon or high-vacuum environment prevents oxidation during the heating comparison.
The proposed behavior may not extend to oxidizing environments or nanoparticles with substantially different sizes.
